newsitem.title: USA: NY Fed's McDonough says Fed should target core CPI.
newsitem.headline: NY Fed's McDonough says Fed should target core CPI.

text.p: Federal Reserve Bank of New York president William McDonough reiterated on Tuesday his view that the Fed should target a range for the core Consumer Price Index (CPI) to achieve price stability.
"Yes, it's targeting core CPI," McDonough told Reuters after addressing a Bank Administration Institute (BAI) conference on the national payment system.
In March, McDonough first said targeting CPI would be an effective means for the central bank to achieve its long-term goal of price stability.
In a speech in New York last week, McDonough refined the concept to target core CPI, the measure of consumer inflation that excludes volatile food and energy prices.
In response to a question, McDonough said targeting core CPI is "a means, not an end" to achieving price stability.
He added that price stability "is a means, not an end, of monetary policy."
"The goal of monetary policy is to achieve long-term sustainable growth," the New York Fed chief added.
Earlier, McDonough told reporters attending the BAI conference that the Fed "strongly believes the way we can bring about growth is by bringing about price stability."

All 19 members of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) have, at times, voiced strong commitments to achieving price stability. However, the Fed has not officially spelled out any numeric definition of price stability.
Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan has described price stability as the stage when inflation gains are so minimal that they no longer affect business or household decisions.
A number of Fed bank presidents, including San Francisco Fed president Robert Parry, have endorsed at least to some extent McDonough's view about targeting core CPI.

Fed officials have said the advantage of setting a target for monetary policy would be to foster transparency at the central bank, and remove some uncertainty in the marketplace about interest rate changes.
McDonough also told reporters the Fed is not in the business of macro-managing the economy. He declined to forecast U.S. economic performance over the next three months.
